questions.q: Identify the tense-aspect of the verb form "pyrs" in the line "iqQVikFk ij pyrs pyrs pyrs" from the poem "olar vk;k" and state whether it is standard Khari Boli or dialectal.
questions.a: Correct: "pyrs" is present habitual aspect, dialectal (Braj/Awadhi region) form corresponding to standard Khari Boli "chalta hai / chalte hain". The triplication "pyrs pyrs pyrs" marks iterative aspect — continuous repeated action. A wrong answer (e.g., calling it past tense or standard Hindi) reveals the student cannot distinguish dialectal verb morphology from standard forms, a critical gap for analyzing how the poem constructs rural voice.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet uses the imperative repetition "rksM+ks rksM+ks rksM+ks" at the start of the second poem instead of a single "rksM+ks" or a polite request like "rksM+ksiye".
questions.a: Correct: The triple imperative mimics the rhythmic, physical act of threshing grain — each "rksM+ks" enacts a blow of the flail. It also reflects the collective, urgent voice of the community addressing the farmer, not an individual polite request. A wrong answer focusing only on "emphasis" without linking to the agricultural action or collective voice shows the student treats repetition as mere decoration, not as grammatical enactment of labor.

questions.q: In the line "fe^h esa jl gksxk gh tc og ikslsxh cht dks", identify the grammatical mood of "gksxk" and "ikslsxh", and explain how the conditional structure "gh tc... tb" (implied) shapes the poem's argument about labor and reward.
questions.a: Correct: "gksxk" is future indicative (standard Khari Boli), "ikslsxh" is future subjunctive/conditional (dialectal "ikslsxh" for standard "iksel"). The structure "gh tc... [result]" creates a cause-effect logic: ONLY when the plough shares the burden will the harvest be golden. A wrong answer misidentifying moods or missing the conditional logic reveals inability to see how grammar builds the poem's central thesis: justice in labor relations.

questions.q: Compare the compound formations "pqjeqjk," (pjejkus dh vkok"k) and "enueghuk" (dkenso dk eghuk) from the vocabulary gloss. Analyze how their samasa type (tatpurusha vs. bahuvrihi) reflects different semantic relationships in the rural world the poem depicts.
questions.a: Correct: "pqjeqjk," is tatpurusha (pjejkus dh vkok"k — desire FOR water), showing a direct object relationship — the crow's need is transitive, goal-directed. "enueghuk" is bahuvrihi (dkenso dk eghuk — one WHOSE master is the season), describing the farmer's identity as defined by an external force. A wrong answer confusing the samasa types or missing the semantic contrast shows the student cannot link morphological structure to the poem's portrayal of agency vs. subjugation.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The poet's use of dialectal forms like 'fiQjdh' (for fiQjgjh) and 'ngj&ngj' (for èkèkd&èkèkd) is merely decorative local color." Defend your position with two specific grammatical arguments from the text.
questions.a: Correct: The claim is false. Argument 1: "fiQjdh" (feminine singular perfective participle) and standard "fiQjgjh" differ in aspectual nuance — the dialect form carries completive force tied to the agricultural cycle's finality. Argument 2: "ngj&ngj" (reduplicated adverbial) encodes iterative manner ("slowly, steadily") that standard "hekd&hekd" lacks — the reduplication itself is a grammatical device for durative aspect. A wrong answer accepting the claim reveals the student sees dialect as ornamental, not as a grammatical system with its own aspectual distinctions.

questions.q: Write four lines of a poem in Hindi (Khari Boli or dialect) about a modern urban laborer (delivery driver, construction worker, etc.) that uses: (a) a repeated imperative verb, (b) a dialectal present habitual form, (c) a bahuvrihi compound describing the worker, and (d) a conditional future structure like "gh tc... tb".
questions.a: Expected criteria: (a) Repeated imperative e.g., "chal chal chal" or "kaam kar kar kar"; (b) Dialectal habitual e.g., "bhagat rahat" (Braj) for "bhagta rehta hai"; (c) Bahuvrihi e.g., "petkebhar" (one whose stomach is full — but ironically empty) or "raatbhar" (one of the whole night); (d) Conditional e.g., "gh tc tankhah mile tb ghar jaun". A poor answer using only standard Hindi, missing any element, or treating dialect as slang shows the student cannot productively apply the grammatical tools analyzed in the poems.
